catalog_quote: [Raz 1983 p.7] The accentual system of Tigre cannot be described in terms of word boundaries, as is the case in many languages. This is, firstly, because stress is non-distinctive and shifts easily from one syllable to the other. Secondly, a certain speech rhythm is maintained by means of which the number of prominent stresses in a given utterance determines the length of time it takes to produce the utterance. This means that the time elapsing between two primary stresses is roughly the same, regardless of the number of syllables in between. ... This unit will be called a “stress unit.” ... Its boundaries are two sharp transitions (non-phonemic) between which there occurs at least one prominent stress. Such an arbitrary unit “cuts” words and affixes in such a way that some bound morphemes fall on the “wrong” side of the juncture. ... [p.8, 2.2.4.1(b), interrogatives] The primary stress…
sweep_summary: Tigre (tigr1270) is in the catalog as PHRASAL on Raz 1983 (stress non-distinctive, mobile, organised in stress-timed 'stress units' cutting across words; Elias 2014 corroborates). this search of works with stress in the title produced one title hit, Palmer 1956 ''Openness' in Tigre: A Problem in Prosodic Statement' (BSOAS 18(3): 561-577, doi 10.1017/S0041977X00088054). Its Cambridge Core extract (saved) shows 'prosodic' in the Firthian sense: the paper abstracts a vowel-harmony feature ('openness', sequences of open front vowels), not stress or accent placement. Full text is paywalled (Cambridge PDF link returns the access page; Unpaywall closed; HathiTrust v.18 search-only; nothing on archive.org), so bears_on_catalog = not-read, priority low: at most a passing remark on prominence in the body, and Raz 1983 already covers stress-unit-conditioned vowel realisation. No first-hand stress statement was newly read. The Bulakh 2013 Russian Jazyki mira chapter already held by the project (sec. 2.1.2 p. 220) was read: it states stress in Tigre has not been systematically investigated and, following Raz, is mobile, non-distinctive and phrase-dependent with one stressed syllable per stress unit; it adds that epenthetic final-cluster ə is quite often stressed (nəsə́r). It confirms the PHRASAL coding and does not supersede Raz. look-ups used Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, HathiTrust and archive.org APIs by automated download instead.

new_statements.quote: 2.1.2. Ударение в Т.я. систематически не исследовалось. Согласно описанию Ш. Раза, в диалекте мэнса оно подвижно, не несет смыслоразличительной нагрузки и зависит от позиции слова во фразе: ударные слоги в речевом потоке встречаются через равномерные промежутки времени. Таким образом, фраза оказывается разбита на несколько слоговых цепочек, каждая из которых содержит лишь один ударный слог (такие цепочки Раз называет акцентными единствами): mən sanat šəḥ samānt məʔət wa-saʕā [mən-sɒnɒt-šə́ḥ samā́nt-m(ə)ʔt wa-saʕā́] ‛c тысяча восемьсот девятого года’.
new_statements.translation: 2.1.2. Stress in Tigre has not been systematically investigated. According to Sh. Raz's description, in the Mansa dialect it is mobile, carries no meaning-distinguishing load and depends on the position of the word in the phrase: stressed syllables in connected speech occur at regular intervals of time. Thus the phrase is split into several syllable chains, each of which contains only one stressed syllable (Raz calls such chains stress units): mən sanat šəḥ samānt məʔət wa-saʕā [mən-sɒnɒt-šə́ḥ samā́nt-m(ə)ʔt wa-saʕā́] 'from the year 1809'.

new_statements.reading: Secondary, not first-hand: Bulakh explicitly relays Raz 1983 (the catalog's deciding source) and adds her own assessment that Tigre stress has never been systematically studied. It restates the catalog's classification exactly: stress non-distinctive, mobile, phrase-position dependent, isochronous stress units cutting across words (PHRASAL). One small refinement: epenthetic ə breaking a final cluster is 'quite often' stressed (nəsə́r 'eagle'), and 2.1.3 shows a-allophony conditioned within the stress unit. Confirms the catalog; does not supersede Raz.

sources.quote: An essential part of the prosodic approach is the abstraction of those features that may be regarded as syntagmatic. One feature of this kind is 'vowel harmony'; prosodic analysis is well equipped to deal with this in terms of 'frontness' and 'backness', or 'openness' and 'closeness', these being treated as characteristic of the entire word or of a considerable part of it. In the phonological analysis of Tigre a prosodic feature of this kind may be abstracted, the relevant phonetic observation being that there are sequences of open front vowels, and that within those sequences there are no half open central vowels. It is this feature that is referred to in the title as 'openness'.
sources.locator: Cambridge Core landing page, 'Extract' (first paragraph of the article)
sources.note: 'Prosodic' here is Firthian: the paper abstracts a vowel-harmony feature ('openness' = sequences of open front vowels without half-open central vowels) as a word-level prosody. The extract says nothing about stress or accent placement; the body (pp. 561-577) was not reachable.
